title: Trust and Reliance on AI in Education: AI Literacy and Need for Cognition as Moderators
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ trust in a generative AI assistant relates to their appropriate reliance on the assistant during problem-solving, and whether that relationship differs by learner characteristics. The central question is whether higher trust helps or harms selective use of AI suggestions, especially when the AI sometimes provides intentionally misleading advice.

The study used a single-session laboratory experiment with 432 undergraduate students enrolled in computing-related courses at the University of Florida. Participants completed 14 Python output-prediction problems while interacting with an AI chatbot that delivered a mix of correct and incorrect recommendations and explanations. Reliance was measured behaviorally by whether students accepted correct recommendations and rejected incorrect ones; surveys measured AI literacy, need for cognition, programming self-efficacy, programming literacy, and post-task trust.

Results showed that higher trust was associated with lower appropriate reliance and lower task accuracy, indicating more frequent acceptance of AI suggestions without sufficient discrimination between correct and incorrect advice. The trust–reliance relationship was nonlinear but did not show a clear optimal middle range within the observed data. AI literacy and need for cognition significantly moderated the association: students higher on those traits tended to show better selective reliance when trust was low, but the trust–reliance slope became more negative as those moderator values increased. The paper concludes that instruction and tool design should support more explicit verification of AI outputs during learning tasks.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family conversational generative AI chatbot/assistant.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as an AI chatbot assistant in a single-session laboratory experiment for Python output-prediction problems. The platform integrated OpenAI's API (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125) to generate follow-up responses after the pre-programmed initial recommendations.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 432 undergraduates, higher post-task trust in the AI assistant was associated with lower appropriate reliance on the chatbot's recommendations during Python output-prediction problems. The regression was significant (b = -3.65, SE = 0.39, t(430) = -9.48, p < .001, R2 = .173), indicating less selective acceptance/rejection of correct versus misleading advice.
findings.measure: Appropriate reliance on AI recommendations during programming problem-solving

findings.finding_summary: A quadratic model fit the trust-to-appropriate-reliance relation slightly better than the linear model (R2 = .185 vs. .173; 94R2 = .012). Both the linear trust term (b = -3.18, p < .001) and the squared term (b = 0.56, p = .011) were significant, suggesting a steep decline in appropriate reliance from low to moderate trust that attenuated at higher trust values, but without reversal within the observed range.
findings.measure: Nonlinear association between trust and appropriate reliance

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot/assistant with no uniquely identified commercial product name in the text.
identified_tools.use_case: The study used a general AI chatbot interface with intentionally correct and misleading recommendations to examine selective reliance in a programming task. The paper names the underlying API (OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo-0125) but treats the system functionally as an AI assistant rather than evaluating a distinct branded educational product.

findings.finding_summary: AI literacy significantly moderated the trust-appropriate reliance relationship (interaction b = -1.03, p = .014). The authors report that the conditional trust slope became more negative as AI literacy increased, with estimated slopes of about -3.59 at -1 SD, -4.62 at the mean, and -5.65 at +1 SD AI literacy, suggesting higher AI literacy supported more selective reliance when trust was lower but not when trust was high.
findings.measure: Moderation of the trust-appropriate reliance relationship by AI literacy

findings.finding_summary: Need for cognition also moderated the trust-appropriate reliance relationship (interaction b = -0.99, p = .040). The conditional trust slope was approximately -3.38 at -1 SD, -4.37 at the mean, and -5.36 at +1 SD need for cognition, indicating that more cognitively reflective students showed higher predicted appropriate reliance when trust was low, but the trust-reliance association became more negative as trust increased.
findings.measure: Moderation of the trust-appropriate reliance relationship by need for cognition

findings.finding_summary: Programming self-efficacy did not significantly moderate the trust-appropriate reliance relationship (interaction p = .121), and programming literacy also did not significantly moderate it (interaction p = .437). The authors describe this as limited evidence that these characteristics altered how trust related to appropriate reliance in this task.
findings.measure: Moderation of the trust-appropriate reliance relationship by programming self-efficacy and programming literacy

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-session correlational laboratory experiment with regression and moderation analyses, not a randomized comparison trial. The methodology is clear and the measures are defined, but the evidence is observational rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: The main trust effect is moderate in magnitude (R2 = .173), but the study does not report educational achievement gains from the AI tool itself. The most relevant findings concern reliance behavior and moderator effects, not direct literacy outcomes.
